metadata.name: Acute otitis media
metadata.emergency_level: Routine - recognise mastoiditis and intracranial complications

overview.short_description: Acute infection/inflammation of the middle ear, common in young children, presenting with ear pain, fever and a bulging red eardrum; usually self-limiting.
overview.detailed_description: AOM is one of the most common childhood infections and a frequent reason for antibiotic prescription. Most cases resolve spontaneously; guidelines favour analgesia and safety-netting with no or delayed antibiotics for most, reserving immediate antibiotics for younger/systemically unwell children, bilateral disease in under-2s, or otorrhoea. The key safety task is to recognise mastoiditis and rarer intracranial complications.
overview.pathophysiology: Eustachian tube dysfunction (often after a viral URTI) impairs middle-ear ventilation and drainage; fluid accumulates and becomes infected by bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis) or viruses, causing a bulging, inflamed tympanic membrane; perforation relieves pain with otorrhoea.
overview.etiology: Bacterial and viral middle-ear infection, usually following a URTI; young children predisposed by short horizontal Eustachian tubes.
overview.natural_history: Pain and fever usually settle within 3-7 days; effusion may persist for weeks (otitis media with effusion).
overview.prognosis: Excellent; recurrent AOM and persistent effusion can affect hearing; complications rare.

prevalence.value: Very common in children; most children have at least one episode by school age.

incidence.value: Peaks age 6-24 months; declines with age.

mortality.value: Negligible; deaths only via rare intracranial complications.

epidemiology.age_groups: Predominantly infants/young children; less common in adults.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Nursery/daycare attendance, exposure to tobacco smoke, bottle-feeding lying flat, dummy/pacifier use.
risk_factors.smoking: Passive smoke exposure increases risk in children.
risk_factors.diabetes: Not a major factor (relevant to malignant otitis externa, not AOM).
risk_factors.travel: Air travel can worsen ear pain with Eustachian dysfunction.
risk_factors.genetic_factors: Craniofacial anomalies (e.g., cleft palate, Down syndrome) increase risk.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Recent URTI; allergic rhinitis; adenoidal hypertrophy.

symptoms.symptom: Bulging, red, or cloudy tympanic membrane with reduced mobility

negative_findings.finding: Normal, mobile tympanic membrane on otoscopy/pneumatic otoscopy
negative_findings.why_important: A normal, mobile drum largely excludes AOM
Absence argues strongly against mastoiditis and serious complication

history_questions.question: How old is the child, and is it one or both ears?
history_questions.why_ask: Under-2s with bilateral AOM benefit more from antibiotics

history_questions.question: Any ear discharge, and how unwell is the child?
Any swelling/redness behind the ear or the ear pushed forwards?
Any severe headache, neck stiffness, facial weakness, or drowsiness?
Recurrent episodes or persistent hearing problems?
history_questions.why_ask: Consider otitis media with effusion / referral

physical_examination.expected_finding: Bulging, red/cloudy, immobile tympanic membrane; +/- perforation with discharge

other_diagnostic_tests.tympanometry: Useful for effusion (otitis media with effusion) in follow-up

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: AOM: acute onset of symptoms (ear pain / infant irritability) WITH otoscopic signs of middle-ear inflammation and effusion - a bulging tympanic membrane, or new otorrhoea not due to otitis externa, or a red/cloudy immobile drum.
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: No formal score; diagnosis is otoscopic + clinical.

differential_diagnosis.differences: No acute infection signs/pain, dull retracted drum, chronic
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_exam: Dull, retracted, immobile drum without bulging/erythema
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is there pain/fever, or just reduced hearing?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Pain on moving pinna/tragus, canal swelling/debris, normal drum
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is it painful to pull on the ear/tragus?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Postauricular swelling/redness/tenderness, protruding ear, systemically unwell

differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Persistent unexplained otalgia in adults (exclude head/neck cancer)
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any tooth, jaw, or throat problems?

diagnostic_questions.question: On looking in the ear, is the eardrum bulging/red/immobile, or normal and mobile?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Bulging/immobile TM confirms AOM; normal mobile TM largely excludes it

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there swelling/redness behind the ear or is the ear pushed forwards?

next_best_question.current_situation: Child with ear pain and AOM on otoscopy
next_best_question.question: How old is the child, is it bilateral, is there discharge, and how unwell are they?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Well, >2y, unilateral, no otorrhoea -> analgesia + no/delayed antibiotics + safety-net; <2y bilateral, otorrhoea, or systemically unwell -> immediate antibiotics; mastoid/neuro red flags -> urgent referral

next_best_test.test: CT temporal bone/brain (only if complication suspected)

red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent - suspected mastoiditis; refer for imaging/IV antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, neck stiffness, facial palsy, drowsiness, or seizures
Systemically very unwell / signs of sepsis, especially in infants
Immunocompromised child or failure to improve on antibiotics

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected mastoiditis/intracranial complication; systemically unwell infant.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Recurrent AOM or persistent otitis media with effusion causing hearing/developmental concern (ENT for grommets consideration).

late: Otitis media with effusion / hearing loss

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance (most resolve spontaneously); adequate analgesia is the priority.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; Ibuprofen/NSAID; Amoxicillin; Macrolide. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG91.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Avoid smoke exposure; keep the ear dry if perforated/discharging.
initial_management.follow_up: Safety-net for mastoid/neurological red flags or failure to improve in 3 days; review persistent effusion/hearing.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain/fever. Antibiotics NOT routinely needed for most; use no-antibiotic or delayed (back-up) prescribing with safety-net advice. Offer IMMEDIATE antibiotics (amoxicillin first-line; macrolide if penicillin-allergic) for children who are systemically very unwell, at higher risk, under 2 with bilateral AOM, or with otorrhoea (NICE NG91).

patient_education.home_advice: Ear infections are common in children and usually clear up on their own within a few days. The most important thing is regular pain relief (paracetamol or ibuprofen). Antibiotics are often not needed. See a doctor urgently if there is swelling or redness behind the ear, the ear is pushed forward, severe headache, a stiff neck, drowsiness, or your child is very unwell.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهابات الأذن شائعة عند الأطفال وتتحسّن غالباً وحدها خلال أيام. الأهم هو تسكين الألم بانتظام (باراسيتامول أو إيبوبروفين)، والمضادات الحيوية كثيراً ما لا تلزم. راجع الطبيب فوراً إذا حدث تورّم أو احمرار خلف الأذن، أو دُفعت الأذن للأمام، أو صداع شديد، أو تيبّس الرقبة، أو خمول، أو إذا كان الطفل متوعّكاً جداً.
patient_education.prevention: Avoid tobacco smoke, keep vaccinations up to date (pneumococcal), breastfeeding where possible.
patient_education.warning_signs: Swelling/redness behind the ear, ear pushed forward, severe headache, neck stiffness, facial weakness, drowsiness, or a very unwell child.

prevention.vaccination: Pneumococcal (and influenza) vaccination reduce some episodes.
prevention.lifestyle: Reduce smoke exposure; breastfeeding; avoid flat bottle-feeding.

evidence.evidence_level: High - most AOM resolves without antibiotics; analgesia is key.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG91; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.

limitations: Guidelines require individual clinical judgement and may differ by country, formulary and antimicrobial resistance.
The evidence audit verifies traceability and major safety structure; it does not certify every narrative sentence.
No medication should be selected or dosed without patient-specific contraindication and interaction checking.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Control pain and reserve antibiotics for people likely to benefit.
treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; Ibuprofen/NSAID; Amoxicillin; Macrolide. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG91.
required_history_before_any_medication: age and weight where dosing is weight- or age-dependent
pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances
major cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bleeding history
non_drug_measures: Observation or delayed prescribing is appropriate for many patients; provide explicit return precautions.

medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: severe active liver disease or prior serious reaction
use_caution_if: heavy alcohol use, malnutrition, low body weight, or concomitant paracetamol-containing products
monitoring: total daily exposure and clinical response

monitoring: renal function, blood pressure, oedema and gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms when clinically indicated
